idiom_name: properties + verb methods + affirmative booleans (Framework Design Guidelines)
implementation_notes: The Framework Design Guidelines replace an interface full of `GetX()`/`SetX()` pairs with C# properties: state appears as nouns (`order.Total`, `order.Lines`), behaviour as verb phrases (`order.AddLine(...)`, `order.Cancel()`), and booleans are affirmative (`IsCancellable`, never `CantCancel`), while the ban on abbreviations, Hungarian notation and language-specific type names keeps the representation out of the name. Named arguments carry the parameter roles when a call site needs them (`order.AddLine(sku: sku, quantity: qty)`), which is the closest C# gets to mandatory argument labels, and records add a cheap intention-revealing value type (`Money Total`, `readonly record struct Quantity`). Keep the plain `GetX` shape only where an external convention expects it - COM interop, `IEnumerable.GetEnumerator`, indexer-heavy collection types, or data-binding paths.
pitfalls: Property getters are expected to be cheap and side-effect-free; an EF Core style property that lazily hits the database is the classic name-lies-about-cost violation - expose it as `LoadAsync()`/`GetX()` instead.
Renaming a public property or method is a binary-breaking change for data binding, serializers and compiled consumers, so plan `[Obsolete]` plus a forwarding member rather than a silent rename.

Positional record parameters become part of the public surface (`with` expressions, deconstruction), so they must be named as carefully as method parameters - `record Order(CartId CartId, BuyerId Buyer)` beats `record Order(Guid a, Guid b)`.
